lesson.title: How AI sees
lesson.subtitle: Pictures are numbers, and AI learns patterns in them

video.title: How AI sees
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — science teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — teacher at the same school (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Where you meet it, and how it’s fooled

scenes.visual: The school garden. Mr Okafor holds his phone over a leaf on a bush; the screen shows the plant’s name a second later. He lowers the phone and looks at the camera lens, puzzled and amused.
scenes.animation: Scan line sweeps over the leaf (1 s); the name card pops up; push-in on Mr Okafor’s curious face.
scenes.narration: I pointed my phone at this leaf, and in one second it told me the plant’s name. But a phone has no eyes like ours. So what does it actually see?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and the AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how AI sees, and why it sometimes sees wrong.

scenes.visual: A photo of the leaf zooms in until it breaks into a grid of squares. One square is picked out and turns into a number; a small black-and-white picture beside it shows 0 on white squares and 9 on the darkest.
scenes.animation: Steady zoom (2 s) until the squares appear; numbers fade into the squares row by row.
scenes.on_screen_text: A picture: a grid of pixels
scenes.narration: Zoom right into any photo, and it breaks into tiny squares called pixels. To a computer, each pixel is just a number. In a simple black-and-white picture, zero could mean white and nine the darkest black. So the picture is a grid of numbers.

scenes.visual: One colour pixel splits into three small bars: red, green and blue, each with its own number. Then the phone photo fills with millions of tiny pixels, and a counter runs up to 36 million.
scenes.animation: The three bars rise (300 ms each); the counter spins up quickly.
scenes.narration: Colour pictures need three numbers for every pixel: how much red, green and blue. A phone photo has about twelve million pixels. That’s thirty-six million numbers in a single photo!

scenes.visual: Clean card with the AI chip. A stack of labelled photos (leaf, ball, face) feeds a chain: edges, then shapes, then whole things, each step drawn simply in ink.
scenes.animation: Each step of the chain appears in turn, arrows drawing between them.
scenes.narration: So computer vision is AI that learns patterns in those numbers. It trains on thousands of labelled photos: leaf, ball, face. First it learns edges, where the numbers jump from light to dark. Then shapes, then whole things.

scenes.visual: A football stadium. Up close, fans each hold up one coloured card. The camera pulls back across the pitch, and the cards form a giant flag.
scenes.animation: Slow pull-back (2 s) as the flag appears.
scenes.narration: Think of fans in a stadium, each holding up one coloured card. Up close, you just see cards. From across the pitch, they make a giant flag. A single pixel means nothing either: the picture is in the pattern.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor takes a photo of the class. Three answer cards drop in beside him.
scenes.animation: Camera flash; Mr Okafor slides in; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! When you take a photo, what does the computer actually get?

scenes.visual: The ‘A grid of numbers’ card gets a check badge. The class photo dissolves into rows of numbers; name tags and speech bubbles fall away from it.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the photo dissolves into numbers (1 s).
scenes.narration: A grid of numbers, and nothing else. No names, no meaning. Everything it “sees” is a pattern it learned in those numbers.

scenes.visual: Three cards: a phone unlocking with a glance; a farmer’s phone over a cassava leaf with a ‘sick leaf’ badge; a phone camera over a street sign, the translation laid on top.
scenes.animation: Each card flips in from the side, about two seconds each.
scenes.narration: You meet vision AI more than you think. Face unlock checks the patterns in your face. Farm apps spot sick leaves on cassava and maize. And camera translation reads a sign, then translates it. Every one starts by turning the picture into numbers.

scenes.visual: The same leaf three times: in dim light (a dark photo), from a strange angle (tilted, half hidden), and a fruit the model never saw, which it labels with the nearest thing it knows and a question mark.
scenes.animation: Each picture slides in; the wrong label wobbles.
scenes.narration: But vision AI can be fooled. Dim light or harsh sun changes every number. A strange angle changes the shapes. And if it never saw something in training, like a fruit that only grows near you, it can only guess the nearest thing it knows.

scenes.visual: The Darsi ‘Images are numbers’ lab on a phone: a 10 by 10 grid with a smile drawn on it, and beside it the same picture as a table of numbers from 0 to 9. A finger taps ‘Darker’, then ‘Move right’, and the numbers change.
scenes.animation: Squares fill as a finger draws; the number table updates after each tap.
scenes.narration: In the lab, draw on a ten-by-ten grid, or start from a smile, a house or a sun. Beside it, you’ll see the same picture as numbers, from zero for white to nine for darkest. Make it darker, lighter, or move it one step, and watch every number change.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina, outside in bright midday sun, holds up a phone that shows ‘Face not recognised’. Two answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Face unlock works every morning in your room. But outside in bright sun, it keeps failing. Why?

scenes.visual: The ‘light changed the numbers’ card gets the check badge, then four summary lines and the takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Points arrive one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: The bright light changed the numbers, so the pattern didn’t match. Remember: a picture is a grid of pixels, and every pixel is a number. Vision AI learns patterns in those numbers from labelled photos. And light, angles and new things can fool it.

scenes.visual: Squared paper with a small picture of a house written only as numbers, 0 and 9. A friend shades the squares from the numbers, and the house appears. Mr Okafor smiles beside them. End card: Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Numbers write themselves in; the friend’s shading reveals the house; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: draw a simple picture on squared paper. Write it as numbers instead, zero for white and nine for black. Give only the numbers to a friend, and see if they can draw your picture back.

checkpoints.prompt: When you take a photo, what does the computer actually get?

options.text: A tiny copy of what we see
The names of things in it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — every pixel is a number. Anything it “sees” is a pattern it learned in those numbers.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the computer gets only numbers, one or three for every pixel. Names come later, from patterns it learned.

checkpoints.prompt: Face unlock works every morning in your room, but keeps failing in bright sun outside. Why?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — bright light changes every pixel’s number, so the pattern no longer matches the one it knows.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it didn’t forget anything. Bright light changed the pixel numbers, so the pattern didn’t match.
